title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
interviewTips: Ask if lists are sorted ascending and if you should reuse existing nodes vs create new nodes
Trade-off: iterative O(1) space is safest for interviews; recursion is elegant but risks stack overflow on very long lists
Edge-case tip: always test both empty, one empty, duplicates, and unequal lengths; ensure tail.next attaches remainder

approaches.name: Approach 1: Collect, Sort and Rebuild
approaches.intuition: If we ignore that inputs are sorted, we can dump all values into an array, sort it, and rebuild a new sorted list. This is simple and correct but wastes the sorted property.
approaches.theory: Traverse list1 and list2 to collect values into array vals of size n+m. Sort vals in O((n+m) log(n+m)). Create a dummy head and append new ListNodes in sorted order. This does not reuse input nodes and uses extra space for array and new nodes.

code.python:
class Solution:
    def mergeTwoLists(self, list1, list2):
        vals = []
        cur = list1
        while cur:
            vals.append(cur.val)
            cur = cur.next
        cur = list2
        while cur:
            vals.append(cur.val)
            cur = cur.next
        vals.sort()
        dummy = ListNode(-1)
        tail = dummy
        for v in vals:
            tail.next = ListNode(v)
            tail = tail.next
        return dummy.next

timeComplexity.explanation: Collecting is O(n+m) and sorting dominates with O((n+m) log(n+m)) where n,m are lengths of the two lists.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Extra array for all values plus new nodes for rebuilt list; does not reuse input nodes.

steps: rebuild new list node by node -> [1,1,2,3,4,4]

edgeCases: one list empty -> returns sorted copy of other

approaches.name: Approach 2: Iterative Merge with Dummy Node
approaches.intuition: Since both lists are already sorted, compare heads and splice the smaller node into the result. A dummy head removes special-casing the first node.
approaches.theory: Maintain tail pointer starting at dummy. While both lists non-empty, attach smaller head to tail.next and advance that list and tail. When one list exhausts, attach the remainder directly since it is already sorted. This reuses existing nodes with in-place splicing and is the standard two-pointer merge like in merge sort.

timeComplexity.explanation: Each node visited once and attached in O(1); total linear in sum of lengths.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only dummy and tail pointers; merging reuses input nodes in place, no extra allocation except dummy.

steps: compare 4 vs 4, take list1 4, attach remainder [4]

edgeCases: different lengths -> remainder attached without loop
equal values -> stable pick from list1 to preserve order

approaches.name: Approach 3: Recursion
approaches.intuition: Merging sorted lists has optimal substructure: the smallest head plus the merge of the rest. Recurse on the remainder.
approaches.theory: Base cases: if list1 is null return list2, if list2 is null return list1. Otherwise if list1.val <= list2.val, set list1.next = merge(list1.next, list2) and return list1, else set list2.next = merge(list1, list2.next) and return list2. Each call reduces total size by one, depth equals n+m in worst case.

timeComplexity.explanation: One recursive call per node, each doing O(1) comparison and pointer assignment.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Recursion call stack depth up to n+m in worst case; O(1) extra heap space as nodes are reused.

edgeCases: both null -> return null without recursion
very long lists may cause stack overflow in C++/Java/Python -> prefer iterative
single-node lists handled by base case
